rv.q: Naturally, in a production that sprints through so many songs and shows in a mere 90 minutes, some numbers provide fewer laughs per bar of music. But the targeting in this outing, subtitled “Merrily We Stole a Song” in a nod to the flood of Sondheim revivals, including “Merrily We Roll Along,” is too often hazy.
Forbidden Broadway is a goof, but a virtuosic and stylish one, with infectious comic verve and lyrics that range from wittily inspired to boldly dumb (rhyming “earplugs” with “queer drugs”).
This edition of Forbidden Broadway is as refreshing as it is hysterical.
Having this much fun is never a crime -- nor should it ever be forbidden!
Even a lower-rung Forbidden Broadway is the equivalent of an upper-rung anything else.
But on the whole, this iteration succeeds in finding more to say about the ridiculousness of Broadway’s current slate.
Still other numbers, parodying such current shows as Hell’s Kitchen and Suffs, feel more obligatory than inspired.
Though its commentary may run dry, Merrily We Stole A Song and its comic cast pluck worthwhile laughs and can satisfy one's thirst for theatre lampoons.
Though the percentage of effective material seems outdone by the percentage of less than par material, much of it sparkles, all the same.
The latest edition of Forbidden Broadway finds its solid footing in a formula that just keeps giving, until it basically hurts.
The full company on “Bump-A-Knee” from Company, Great Gatsby for Dummies and Hayward on Cabaret‘s “Wilkommen” is hilarious...
Alessandrini's insidery lyrics are the real star here, and they remain caustic fun.
With more than two dozen numbers, not all of Forbidden Broadway tickles the funny bone, and Alessandrini’s cultural references could use a jolt to attract a new generation of theatergoers.
Forbidden Broadway is a goof, but a virtuosic and stylish one, with infectious comic verve and lyrics that range from wittily inspired to boldly dumb.

cn.t: Alessandrini's long-running Broadway parody franchise returns with sharp wit and a talented cast, though the satirical hits are uneven. Critics praise the virtuosic performances and punchy humor, but note some jokes miss their mark.
